title: Why Do We Lose Our Sense of Wonder?
metaTitle: Why Do We Lose Our Sense of Wonder?
metaDescription: Wonder fades mostly through habituation — the brain dials down its response to the familiar. But it is recoverable, and awe appears to be good for us.
keyFinding: We lose our sense of wonder largely because the brain habituates to the familiar, so the everyday stops feeling remarkable — but wonder is recoverable, and awe appears to benefit wellbeing.
honestAnswer: We mostly lose wonder through habituation: the brain is built to dial down its response to things it has already seen, so the familiar quietly stops registering as remarkable. A child's wonder partly reflects newness — almost everything is encountered for the first time — while an adult has filed most of the world under 'already known.' Add routine, screens that crowd out fresh experience, and busyness, and the everyday flattens into background.

The encouraging part is that this is not a permanent loss. Wonder and its bigger cousin, awe, appear to be recoverable through deliberate exposure to novelty, nature, art, and a 'fresh eyes' way of looking. Research also suggests awe is genuinely good for us — linked to greater wellbeing, humility, and connection — so rekindling it is worth doing rather than merely nostalgic.
whatDataShows: The core mechanism is habituation, one of the most basic and well-established features of the nervous system: when a stimulus repeats, our response to it weakens. This is adaptive — it frees attention for what is new or threatening — but it means that repeated exposure to almost anything, however beautiful, gradually mutes its impact. The same sunset, commute, or relationship cue that once stopped you starts to disappear into routine.

Awe — the feeling of wonder in the presence of something vast, novel, or hard to fit into our existing mental categories — has been studied extensively by Dacher Keltner and colleagues. Their research associates experiences of awe with higher wellbeing, greater humility, a sense of being part of something larger, and stronger feelings of connection to others. In this account, wonder is not a frill; it is tied to how we relate to the world and each other.

Keltner's work also points to why adults seem to feel it less: awe depends partly on novelty and vastness, and adult life tends to be saturated with the familiar and increasingly mediated through screens, which can crowd out the kinds of direct, novel, expansive experiences that trigger it. Children, encountering more of the world for the first time, have novelty working in their favour by default.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It can feel as though the world itself has become less wondrous — duller, smaller, more predictable — when what has actually changed is your response to it. Habituation operates quietly and automatically, so the fading registers as a property of the world rather than of your own attention. The sunset is the same; your brain has simply stopped flagging it.

It can also feel like wonder is a childish thing you are supposed to outgrow, which makes its loss seem natural and even appropriate. But the research suggests children's wonder is driven substantially by newness rather than by some special capacity that adults lack, and that adults can deliberately recreate the conditions for it.

And modern life makes the loss easy to miss, because screens supply a constant stream of mild, manufactured novelty that feels like stimulation without producing the expansive, hard-to-categorise quality of real awe. The feed is busy, so it does not feel like anything is missing — even as the deeper experience of wonder gets crowded out.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most direct implication of the awe research is to seek out the conditions that produce it: nature, especially vast or open settings; art and music; genuinely new experiences; and moments of scale that don't fit neatly into your existing categories. Because awe depends on novelty and vastness, deliberately exposing yourself to those tends to rekindle it.

A 'fresh eyes' stance helps counter habituation directly. Slowing down and attending to the familiar as if encountering it for the first time — sometimes called savouring — can partly reverse the automatic muting, restoring some of the impact routine has worn away. Practices like awe walks, in which people deliberately attend to the novel and vast around them, have been studied in this vein.

Reducing screen saturation also appears to matter, because the constant manufactured novelty of feeds can crowd out the direct, expansive experiences awe depends on. Making room — unstructured time, real-world novelty, contact with the natural and the large — is the broad pattern the research supports for getting wonder back.
whatDoesNotHelp: Chasing ever-bigger thrills or constant consumer novelty tends not to restore wonder, because habituation catches up quickly — each new purchase or stimulus fades into baseline much as the last did. The treadmill of more does not deliver the durable, expansive quality of awe.

Scrolling for novelty is a poor substitute. The manufactured, bite-sized stimulation of feeds can feel like wonder-adjacent excitement while actually crowding out the direct, vast, hard-to-categorise experiences the awe research associates with real benefits.

Waiting passively for wonder to return on its own is unlikely to work, given that habituation is automatic and routine reinforces it. The research suggests wonder is recovered through deliberate exposure to novelty and a fresh-eyes attention, not by hoping the world will start feeling magical again by itself.
realNumbersInContext: This is a topic carried by mechanisms rather than precise statistics, so the honest anchors are two well-supported ideas: habituation, the nervous system's basic tendency to respond less to repeated stimuli, and Dacher Keltner's body of research on awe. Habituation explains the fading; the awe literature explains why getting wonder back is worth the effort.

What Keltner's work reasonably supports is that experiences of awe are associated with higher wellbeing, greater humility, and stronger feelings of connection, and that they depend partly on novelty and vastness — which is why routine and screens, by reducing both, tend to reduce awe. These are well-supported tendencies rather than precise effect sizes, and wonder appears to be recoverable rather than permanently lost.

faqs.question: Why does the world feel less wondrous as I get older?
faqs.answer: Mostly because of habituation: the brain responds less to things it has seen before, so the familiar stops registering as remarkable. It can feel like the world has changed when what has changed is your automatic response to it. Routine and screens reinforce the effect by reducing the novelty that wonder depends on.

faqs.question: Is awe actually good for you?
faqs.answer: Dacher Keltner's research associates experiences of awe with higher wellbeing, greater humility, a sense of being part of something larger, and stronger connection to others. The effects are well-supported tendencies rather than guarantees, but the direction is consistent: awe appears to be genuinely beneficial, not just pleasant.

faqs.question: Can you get your sense of wonder back?
faqs.answer: The research suggests yes. Because wonder fades through habituation rather than being permanently lost, deliberately seeking novelty, nature, art, and moments of scale — and attending to the familiar with 'fresh eyes' — can rekindle it. It tends to take some intention rather than returning on its own.

faqs.question: Why do children seem to feel more wonder than adults?
faqs.answer: Largely because so much of the world is new to them, and awe depends partly on novelty. Children have newness working in their favour by default, while adults have filed most things under 'already known.' This suggests the difference is less about a special childhood capacity and more about how much novelty each is encountering.

faqs.question: Do screens reduce our sense of wonder?
faqs.answer: The awe research suggests they can, by crowding out the direct, vast, novel experiences that trigger awe and replacing them with constant manufactured novelty that feels stimulating but is more easily habituated. Making room for real-world novelty and nature is part of the pattern the research supports for restoring wonder.

dataSources: Dacher Keltner — research on awe, its triggers (vastness and novelty), and its links to wellbeing, humility, and connection.
Habituation / sensory adaptation — the well-established tendency of the nervous system to respond less to repeated stimuli.
Research on awe and wellbeing — including practices such as awe walks and savouring.
